parakeet: What if holidays were never actually about doctrine? What if what we now call Easter celebrations originated around something far more human? Survival, cooperation, seasonal change, food cycles, memory, and hope. And what if religion didn't invent those gatherings so much as absorbed them, reinterpret them, and slowly convince people that the meaning of the ritual belonged to heaven more than to humanity? Because one of the biggest costs of superstition is not just that it gives people bad explanations, it disconnects us from our own story. It makes us forget why human beings gathered in the first place, what our ancestors were responding to, and why ritual mattered long before theology tried to own it. Religion didn't just reinterpret holidays, it helped disconnect people from the material, social, and seasonal realities that made ritual necessary in the first place. Holidays were once practical human technologies for survival, memory, cooperation, transition, and meaning making. Religious systems often mythologized those rhythms so heavily that people became more loyal to supernatural explanations than to the actual human story those rituals were helping communities navigate. The supernatural explanation becomes official, and everything else gets pushed to the margins. What may have once been open, communal, adaptive, and connected to human life becomes enclosed inside sacred narratives. We're no longer just talking about celebration, we're talking about interpretive control. The real issue is the way religious frameworks can take custody of shared human practices and then treat alternative readings, historical, social, natural, or human-centered ones, as if they're shallow, rebellious, or incomplete. For communities living much closer to the earth than most of us do now, these changes were not minor. They affected survival, labor, mood, planning, and social organization all at once. That's why seasonal gatherings mattered. They gave communities a way to respond together to change instead of experiencing it in isolation. And once you understand that, you can see the deeper loss that happens when those practices get explained only through sacred stories. Because then people may continue the outward celebration while losing sight of the human conditions that made the celebration meaningful in the first place. What was once connected to season, labor, uncertainty, survival, and renewal becomes detached from those realities and absorbed into metaphysical narrative. And once that happens, people can participate in the ritual without understanding what problem it originally helped human communities solve. When religious frameworks take over human rituals, they do more than change the story. We stop seeing ritual as something human communities develop in response to real conditions, real fears, real hopes, real transitions, and real needs. We inherit the practice but lose contact with the problem it was helping people solve.
